gaps.old_draft_snippet: Unlike interferometric architectures that rely on precise phase matching between two arms, resonant devices depend on constructive interference within a closed loop, making them inherently sensitive to any perturbation that shifts the effective optical path length. Even small temperature variations of a fraction of a degree can detune a resonator from its designed wavelength, causing signal loss or crosstalk between adjacent channels.
gaps.scientific_content: The specific physical mechanism distinguishing resonant vulnerability from interferometric stability: resonators rely on constructive interference in a closed loop (effective optical path length), whereas interferometers rely on phase matching between two arms. This explains why sub-degree temperature fluctuations cause resonant detuning and channel crosstalk.

gaps.old_draft_snippet: When both physical and geometrical degrees of freedom are large and strongly coupled, the curse of dimensionality becomes significant, requiring PDE-based constraints to provide useful inductive bias for physically consistent learning.
gaps.scientific_content: The condition under which PDE-based constraints are necessary for inductive bias: specifically when physical and geometrical degrees of freedom are large and strongly coupled, leading to the curse of dimensionality.

gaps.old_draft_snippet: Higher dimensional data such as field intensity profiles as well as vectorial field maps carry much more information that can be used for designing functional metalenses and holograms.
gaps.scientific_content: The limitation of current deep learning inverse design to low-dimensional inputs (spectra/diffraction efficiencies) and the potential benefit of using higher-dimensional data (field intensity profiles, vectorial field maps) for designing complex devices like metalenses and holograms.
